issues.description: The UML in the problem statement defines Animal with two attributes (name: String and age: int) and a constructor Animal(String, int), but the actual code examples and the solution use a single-parameter constructor (Animal(String)) and do not include an age attribute. This mismatch between the specification (problem_statement.md) and the provided solution/template Main usage will confuse students about which constructor and attributes they must implement.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the specification, template, and solution. Either (A) update the problem statement/UML to show Animal only needs a name and a constructor Animal(String) (remove the age attribute and the two-argument constructor), or (B) update the solution/template to include the age attribute and provide constructors Animal(String, int) (and change Seal/Pig/Goat constructors and the Main instantiations accordingly). Ensure the tasks and example usages in Main match the chosen constructor signature.

issues.description: The UML in the problem statement specifies Animal has an 'age' attribute and a constructor Animal(String, int), but both the template usage (Main.java) and the solution implementation use a single-argument constructor Animal(String) and do not define an 'age' attribute. This mismatch between the UML/spec and the code can confuse students about the required constructor signature and attributes of Animal.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the specification and code consistent. Either (A) update the UML/problem statement to remove the 'age' attribute and the Animal(String, int) constructor so it expects Animal(String), or (B) extend the template and solution to include the 'age' attribute and change constructors in Animal and all subclasses to Animal(String, int) (and update Main.java usages accordingly). Ensure the problem text, UML, template examples, and solution use the same constructor signature and attribute set.
